chosen: Treatment and imaging day are perfectly confounded in this pilot, so the current data cannot identify a treatment effect separately from a day effect. A regression or mixed model can label both variables, but with no within-day treatment overlap it cannot create the missing information. The next step is a crossed or blocked experiment in which treated and control samples are represented on the same days (ideally randomized within day/plate), with the same acquisition and segmentation pipeline. The pilot can motivate that replication and support QC checks, but it should not be reported as isolating treatment from day.
prompt: A pilot study compares a new cell-culture treatment with control. All treated plates were imaged on Tuesday and all control plates on Monday because of scheduling constraints. The effect is large. What can the current data establish, and what design or analysis step is needed before attributing the difference to treatment?
rejected: Fit a model with treatment and imaging day as separate covariates. If the treatment coefficient remains statistically significant after adding day, the day effect has been controlled and the treatment difference can be attributed to the intervention.

chosen: First quantify the diagnosis-scanner association and test whether scanner identity itself predicts the label. Evaluate the classifier within scanner where both labels are present, and use a scanner-stratified or leave-scanner-out evaluation only where the data support it. Inspect saliency/error patterns cautiously and compare performance after harmonized preprocessing. Most importantly, collect or identify a dataset with label overlap across scanners—positive and negative cases on each scanner—because near-complete scanner-label confounding cannot be resolved by post-hoc adjustment alone. Report performance by scanner and uncertainty rather than a pooled headline metric.
prompt: A hospital classifier appears more accurate for one diagnosis group, but nearly all positive cases came from Scanner A and nearly all negative cases from Scanner B. Images and scanner metadata are available. Propose a validation strategy that tests whether the model learned disease signal rather than scanner identity.
rejected: Randomly shuffle scanner labels many times while keeping diagnosis labels fixed. If the classifier's accuracy stays high across those permutations, scanner effects have been ruled out and the remaining performance must come from disease morphology.

chosen: A simple before/after contrast is confounded with time because treatment status is determined by clock time. Examine historical within-day patterns and traffic composition as diagnostics, but those adjustments do not fully identify the causal effect. The clean follow-up is a randomized concurrent holdout or staggered rollout that creates treated and untreated users over the same time windows. If operationally possible, randomize at user or session level and predefine the conversion metric. Until then, describe the noon discontinuity as an association, not a causal lift.
prompt: An online product change was enabled for all users at noon. Conversion after noon is higher than conversion before noon. No simultaneous control group exists. How should the team distinguish a product effect from time-of-day or traffic-composition effects?
rejected: Add hour-of-day and traffic-source covariates to a logistic regression. If the product-change coefficient is positive and significant, the model has separated the rollout effect from all time-related confounding and establishes causal lift.

chosen: Because disease status and batch are perfectly aligned, their effects are not separately identifiable from these data. Including both columns in a design matrix produces collinearity rather than new information, and aggressive batch correction risks removing real disease signal or preserving batch signal arbitrarily. The defensible next step is to generate or obtain samples that cross disease status with batch—both disease and healthy samples processed across multiple batches—then analyze with the blocking structure specified prospectively. The existing dataset can still be used for QC and hypothesis generation, with the confounding stated explicitly.
prompt: In an RNA-seq experiment, every disease sample was processed in sequencing Batch 1 and every healthy sample in Batch 2. The analysis software can include batch as a covariate. What is the correct interpretation and next step?
rejected: Use a standard batch-correction algorithm before differential-expression testing. Once Batch 1 and Batch 2 are normalized to the same distribution, any remaining expression differences can be interpreted as disease effects.

chosen: The current comparison mixes fertilizer and greenhouse temperature, so it cannot isolate fertilizer. A minimal convincing follow-up crosses the factors: use both fertilizers in each greenhouse, randomize pots to fertilizer within greenhouse, and distribute positions to reduce bench/location effects. With replication in each fertilizer-by-greenhouse cell, estimate the fertilizer effect while accounting for greenhouse and test whether the fertilizer effect changes by greenhouse. If only one greenhouse can be used at a time, repeat both fertilizers within each temperature condition rather than preserving the original one-to-one assignment.
prompt: A greenhouse study compares two fertilizers, but Fertilizer A was used only in the warmer greenhouse and Fertilizer B only in the cooler greenhouse. Plant height differs after four weeks. Design the smallest convincing follow-up.
rejected: Repeat the experiment with more plants but keep Fertilizer A in the warm greenhouse and Fertilizer B in the cool greenhouse. A larger sample size will reduce random error enough to reveal which fertilizer is responsible for the height difference.

chosen: Because the raw images are available, run both the old and new segmentation pipelines on the same image set. Pair the resulting measurements image-by-image (or field-by-field) so acquisition date is held fixed while pipeline changes. Inspect disagreement cases and predefine summary metrics such as median area difference and segmentation QC. If both pipelines can be applied to all images, this crossed reanalysis directly identifies the software effect much better than comparing old-early against new-late outputs. Acquisition-date effects can then be examined separately on the common reprocessed data.
prompt: A microscopy segmentation update seems to reduce measured cell area. However, all images analyzed with the old pipeline were acquired earlier in the month and all images with the new pipeline later. Raw images are available. How can the pipeline effect be isolated without recollecting images?
rejected: Regress measured cell area on pipeline version and acquisition date using the existing outputs. If the pipeline coefficient is significant after adjusting for date, no reprocessing of the same raw images is necessary.
